content: The Montana Meth Project is an anti-drug organization based in Montana, founded by billionaire Thomas Siebel. Its primary focus is an advertising campaign designed to shock and horrify viewers about the potential dangers of methamphetamine use. The advertisements often center on themes of regret, sometimes featuring teens who are not yet addicted encountering their future selves, who warn them about the consequences of their choices. Common elements in these ads include depictions of methamphetamine psychosis, the deterioration of physical health, and the decline in living conditions. By 2007, these advertisements had been adopted in other states, such as Arizona and Idaho. Television Spots All 12 television spots were created by the San Francisco-based advertising agency Venables Bell & Partners. The 2005 and 2006 spots were directed by Tony Kaye, while the 2007 spots were directed by Darren Aronofsky. In the following descriptions, the term meth is used as a shorthand for methamphetamine. 2005-2006: Directed by Tony Kaye Phase I: Bathtub: A teenage girl is taking a shower while waiting for her friend to arrive, presumably to try meth for the first time. During her shower, she turns around and screams when she sees a pockmarked, bleeding version of herself shivering at the bottom of the shower. This future version of herself pleads, Don't do it. Laundromat: A deranged, meth-addicted young man storms into a laundromat, demanding money from everyone inside. He beats a man to the ground and screams in the faces of women and children. He then confronts his pre-addicted self, grabbing him by the collar and shouting, This wasn’t supposed to be your life. Just Once: A teenage girl declares that she will only try meth just once. This leads to a series of escalating compromises to support her addiction, each of which she promises will be just once. The ad ends with her pre-teen sister stealing her drugs and whispering, I’m going to try meth, just once. That Guy: A teenage boy says, I’m going to try meth just once. I’m not going to be like that guy, gesturing toward a future version of himself who deteriorates over time, eventually ending up shaking and sweating on a drug dealer’s couch. A teenage girl then buys meth from the same dealer, saying, I’m going to try meth just once. I’m not going to be like that guy, referring to the now-wretched boy. Phase II: Junkie Den: In a dark, grimy drug den, a young boy tries meth for the first time. He is congratulated by dirty, drug-addicted individuals who describe his future life as one of us and suggest that they will be sleeping together as well. When the boy protests that he is only trying meth once, the group erupts into mocking laughter. Crash: A car is driving in the rain at night when a tire blows out, causing the car to flip over. In narration, the teenage driver wishes she had crashed on her way to that party, even if it meant breaking her neck and becoming paralyzed, because it would have prevented her from trying meth. The ad cuts to her current life as an addict, smoking meth in a filthy, run-down apartment, where she says, Now this is my life. Everything Else: A girl approaches a group of meth users and asks for some meth. The dealer gives her the drug along with everything else that comes with it. This includes an intimidating drug dealer, meth boyfriends who rape her and supply her with meth, an addicted baby, and her reflection in a mirror showing her bleeding meth face. Jumped: A younger teenage boy is chased through a parking lot by three older males who beat him to the ground and kick him. In narration, the boy wishes he had been assaulted that night because it would have prevented him from trying meth. The ad cuts to a drug den, where the boy, now shaking, says, Now all I do is meth. 2007: Directed by Darren Aronofsky Phase III: Boyfriend: A teenage girl is shown lying on a bed in her underwear as an older man zips up his pants and leaves the motel room. In narration, she says, I love my boyfriend. We’ve been together since like 8th grade. He takes care of me. As the older man exits, he hands something to the boyfriend, who is standing outside the door. The boyfriend enters the room and shows her the meth, as she cringes and weeps. Mother: A teenage boy rummages through his mother’s purse for money while narrating how much he loves her. When she enters the room and objects to his theft, both dismayed and concerned for her son, he strikes her to the floor. She cries out to him, clinging to his leg. He kicks free and flees, leaving her sobbing on the floor. Friends: From inside a car, we see a worried passenger, a reckless driver, and a second worried passenger. A female narrator says that she is tight with her friends who always look out for me. The narrator is revealed to be the third passenger, slumped in the backseat. The car pulls up to a hospital emergency room, where her friends dump her unresponsive body on the curb and speed off. Parents: In narration, he talks about how close he has always been with his parents. Inside the house, the parents are panicked and distraught, turning off the lights. The boy kicks the door repeatedly, begging to be let in and screaming that he’s going to kill them. Criticism While many members of the state legislature praise the Montana Meth Project as an unprecedented success—going so far as to fund the previously privately-funded project with tax dollars—some Montana residents believe the project is unlikely to have a significant long-term impact. Critics have labeled the project as employing scare tactics and have criticized its lack of credible scientific evidence to support the claims made in the ads. However, some surveys have suggested that the project is effective, though these surveys have been questioned due to their origin within the project itself. Some view the results as part of a broader trend of declining methamphetamine usage rather than a direct result of the campaign.
